status_flags.finding: Census lists 'operating' with official start of sales; in fact filed for insolvency Dec 9, 2025 (Hamburg District Court, provisional administrator Tjark Thies, ~120 employees) after a failed financing round. Operations continuing while it seeks rescue investors; status should be distressed/uncertain, not clean operating.

Census lists 'operating' with USD 19.1M 2024 revenue; the company filed for bankruptcy (~2025) and is now marked inactive/'deadpooled' by PitchBook, Tracxn and CB Insights. Status should be bankrupt-shutdown — a major correction since it was the longest-running wave-energy player with real revenue.

Operating status correct, but the signal 'Kentucky gigafactory built' is misleading: EnerVenue vacated/abandoned the Kentucky plant in Nov 2024 without ramping (site taken over by Canadian Solar) and moved all high-volume manufacturing to Changzhou, China — which creates FEOC/domestic-content exposure worth noting alongside the $300M Series B.

Needs update and nuance: no longer purely pre-production — first vehicle came off its low-volume validation line Mar 3, 2026, with first customer deliveries targeted late 2026. But Q1 2026 10-Q discloses ~$17.7M cash vs $1.7-2.0M/month burn, management states cash is insufficient for the next 12 months, and it needs another $45-50M for low-volume production ($140-160M for high volume). Operating but with explicit going-concern risk.

'Uncertain' status remains apt but the evidence is stale: as of May-June 2026 ESS is still operating after a ~$31M financing injection, reported Q2 2025 revenue up 578% YoY, won a $9.9M USAF/CTC contract, and acquired insolvent German rival VoltStorage's IP — yet going-concern doubt persists and it says it needs additional debt/equity.

Census flags 'uncertain' — verification supports going further: no primary evidence the company exists (no website, press release, or independent coverage found); the $15M Series A claim traces only to the same Market Research Future agrivoltaics report. Likely a market-report artifact; recommend removing or annotating as unverifiable.

missing.what: JA Solar and Canadian Solar — two of the global top-5 module suppliers (Canadian Solar also a top-10 BESS integrator via e-STORAGE); their absence from the module-maker roster is the most obvious gap a PV analyst would catch.

missing.where: Solar (missing variation): upstream polysilicon/ingot/wafer supply chain
missing.what: Tongwei (world's largest cell/polysilicon maker), GCL Technology, Daqo, Wacker, Hemlock — the census covers no upstream at all, even though polysilicon/wafer is where Chinese concentration risk and the 2024-25 price collapse live (and where REC Silicon's US restart just failed).

missing.where: Solar / distributed & utility-scale (missing variation): PV inverters & power conversion
missing.what: Huawei — the world's No. 1 inverter supplier by shipments — appears nowhere; Sungrow appears only via floating/BESS arms. Inverters/PCS are the decisive electrical BOS layer and a census of solar supply without the Huawei-Sungrow duopoly is visibly incomplete.

missing.where: Wind (missing variation): blade & drivetrain component manufacturing
missing.what: TPI Composites — world's largest independent wind-blade maker, Chapter 11 Aug 2025 (Türkiye plants sold, Vestas stalking-horse for the rest) — plus LM Wind Power (GE) and gearbox makers (ZF/Winergy). The census covers OEMs and blade recycling but skips the component tier whose distress defined 2024-25 wind economics.

EVE Energy (top-2 global ESS cell supplier), HyperStrong (China's No. 1 and a global top-3 BESS integrator), and Wärtsilä ES&O (leading Western integrator alongside Fluence) — all bigger players than several names listed.

missing.where: Electrochemical Storage (missing variation): battery recycling & materials circularity
missing.what: Redwood Materials, Li-Cycle (CCAA May 2025, acquired by Glencore Aug 2025), Ascend Elements, Cirba Solutions — census covers PV recycling, blade recycling and second-life packs but not cell recycling, the largest circularity industry in the sector.

Framatome (EPR co-builder and one of the West's two major fuel/reactor-services firms) and AtkinsRéalis/CANDU Energy (only heavy-water reactor vendor; Candu Monark, Cernavoda units, and the global CANDU refurbishment franchise) are both absent.
Kazatomprom — the world's largest uranium producer (~20%+ of mined supply); listing Cameco alone hides where front-end supply concentration actually sits.

missing.where: Thermal & Mechanical LDES / High-temperature thermal batteries
missing.what: Hyme Energy (Denmark, Seaborg spin-out) — molten hydroxide salt heat storage with industrial pilots (Esbjerg/Bornholm); one of the few credible European molten-salt thermal startups and a natural peer to Kyoto Group/Malta.

Marathon Fusion (San Francisco; tritium fuel-processing/pumping components, venture-funded 2024-25) — directly relevant because the variation's white-space claims tritium handling has 'almost no independent players.'

notable_failures: Meyer Burger — premium European+US heterojunction module manufacturing against Chinese pricing — German/Swiss insolvency and US Chapter 11, >900 layoffs; US assets and patents sold to Swift Solar (2025)
SunPower — once-leading US residential solar sales/dealer platform — Chapter 11; brands and units sold to Complete Solaria for $45M (2024)
Sunnova — major US residential solar TPO financier — Chapter 11 with >$8B liabilities after DOE rescinded its partial loan guarantee (2025)
Titan Solar Power — one of the largest US dealer-model residential installers — abrupt shutdown, then bankruptcy (2024)
Lumio — PE-backed US residential solar installer roll-up — Chapter 11, sold to lender White Oak (2024)
iSun — listed US solar EPC/installer — Chapter 11 and asset sale (2024)
Pink Energy (PowerHome Solar) — US residential installer — abrupt collapse amid state consumer-protection lawsuits (2022)
Sunlight Financial — residential solar loan platform — Chapter 11 and distressed sale (2023)
Toledo Solar — US CdTe thin-film challenger to First Solar — ceased operations after First Solar IP lawsuit (2024)
REC Silicon — restart of US granular polysilicon (Moses Lake) for a domestic solar supply chain — failed product qualification, plant shut, exited polysilicon (2024-25)
Ubiquitous Energy — transparent solar-window coatings (>$70M raised) — staff terminated and wound down (2024)
Lightyear — solar passenger car — bankrupt weeks after starting production; IP pivot never scaled (2023)
Sono Motors — Sion solar car — program cancelled after ~$330M spent; company survived only by shrinking to solar retrofit kits for buses/vans (2023)
ASCA (Armor Group) — roll-to-roll printed organic PV films — liquidated by Armor on poor cost/return; brand and IP picked up by construction firm Hering Group (2023)
Ampyx Power — utility-scale rigid-wing airborne wind — bankrupt after ~EUR 50M raised vs ~EUR 500M need; concept continued by successor Mozaero (2023)
SkySails Power — closest-to-market airborne wind kite systems — filed for insolvency in Hamburg while seeking rescue investors (2025)
TPI Composites — world's largest independent wind turbine blade maker — Chapter 11 in Texas; Turkish plants sold, Vestas stalking-horse for remaining assets (2025)
Sustainable Marine Energy — floating tidal platforms, first floating tidal power to Canada's grid — withdrew from Bay of Fundy project blaming permitting, entered administration (2023)
Wello Oy — Penguin rotating-mass wave converter — bankruptcy after two full-scale devices failed at sea (2023)
AW-Energy — WaveRoller nearshore wave converter, the sector's longest-running revenue-generating player — filed for bankruptcy (2025)
Ultra Safe Nuclear Corporation — gas-cooled microreactors and TRISO fuel — Chapter 11 mid-demonstration; fuel assets reborn as Standard Nuclear (2024)
U-Battery — 4 MWe HTGR microreactor consortium — wound down after Urenco found no commercial investors; IP to UK NNL (2023)
NuScale/UAMPS Carbon Free Power Project — first NRC-licensed US SMR deployment — cancelled on cost escalation, the SMR demand-side cautionary tale (2023)
Northvolt — Europe's flagship battery manufacturer incl. its largest BESS systems plant — bankruptcy; factories acquired by Lyten (2024-25)
Morrow Batteries — Norwegian LFP cell maker targeting stationary storage — filed for bankruptcy (2025)
Powin — top-3 US grid BESS integrator (11+ GWh installed) — Chapter 11; assets sold to FlexGen for $36M (2025)
Natron Energy — US sodium-ion pioneer for data-center power — shut down after funding fell through; $1.4B NC gigafactory cancelled (2025)
Redflow — Australian zinc-bromine flow batteries — voluntary administration, then liquidation (2024)
VoltStorage — German flow/iron-salt battery maker (EUR 66M raised) — insolvency and wind-down; IP and team acquired by ESS Tech (2024-25)
Ambri — calcium-antimony liquid-metal battery — Chapter 11, emerged under lender consortium at reduced scale (2024)
Moxion Power — mobile battery rental units for diesel-generator replacement — Chapter 7 shutdown after ~$110M raised (2024)
Britishvolt — UK 30+ GWh gigafactory venture — administration with minimal assets (2023)
Freyr Battery — Norwegian battery gigafactories — abandoned cell manufacturing entirely, pivoted to US solar as T1 Energy (2024-25)
Li-Cycle — North American lithium battery recycler (Rochester hub) — CCAA/Chapter 15 creditor protection; sold to Glencore for ~$40M vs ~$1B+ invested (2025)
Azelio — aluminum-alloy PCM storage with Stirling-engine output — abrupt bankruptcy after failing to raise (2023)
Heliogen — AI-aligned heliostat CSP SPAC valued ~$2B — demos cancelled, wound down into distressed sale to Zeo Energy (2025)
NGK Insulators (NAS line) — sole mass producer of sodium-sulfur grid batteries for 20+ years (~5 GWh fielded) — discontinued NAS manufacturing and new orders after BASF partnership talks ended (2025)
Corre Energy — listed European salt-cavern CAES developer — Dutch operating subsidiary bankrupt, group in distressed investor search (2025)
First Light Fusion — projectile-driven fusion power plants — abandoned its power-plant route, valuation cut >60%, pivoted to selling amplifier/target tech to other programs (2025)
